title: Making a Living Making Games | What Do Designers, Programmers, and Artists Do?

scenes.title: The People Who Make Games
lines: If you love games, what do the people who make them actually do?
Behind every game screen are people responsible for very different kinds of work.
Someone defines the rules of play, and someone else makes those rules work for real.
Others draw the world, build it in three dimensions, and give it movement.
Today we will focus on game designers, programmers, 2D artists, and 3D artists.
We will see what each group makes, who they work with, and which fundamentals are useful at the start.
Job names and boundaries vary between companies and projects.
Think of these categories as a map for finding your preferred work, not as a fixed answer sheet.

scenes.title: Four Views of One Scene
lines: Imagine a player discovering and opening a treasure chest.
A designer decides why the player should want to open it and what reward it should contain.
A programmer makes the lid open and the reward appear when the player gives an input.
A 2D artist designs the chest's appearance, icons, and visual information on screen.
A 3D artist builds the chest in space and connects its materials and motion to the game.
It is a short moment for the player, but a meeting point for several people's work.
One person may cover several roles on a small team, while a large team may split them further.
No role sits above the others; they solve different problems together.

scenes.title: Game Designer — Designing the Player Experience
lines: A game designer shapes what the player sees, chooses, learns, and feels.
A systems designer may create combat rules or progression structures.
A level designer works with spaces and routes, while UI and UX designers shape interaction flows.
The job does not end with having an idea.
Designers communicate it through documents, tables, simple diagrams, and prototypes so the team can build the same thing.
They play the result, check whether the intended fun appears, and tune the values.
Core skills include analyzing games, writing clearly, and listening to other people.
Spreadsheets and basic engine skills also help designers test ideas quickly.
A strong designer is less a person who dictates answers and more a person who makes the team's problem clear.

scenes.title: Game Programmer — Making the Rules Work
lines: Game programmers implement systems so design and art can function inside the game.
Gameplay programmers may build movement and combat.
Others specialize in graphics, engines, physics, tools, networking, or servers.
For a chest, the programmer connects input, opening conditions, and reward storage.
They trace and fix incorrect or slow behavior, and may build tools that help the rest of the team work.
At the beginning, learning program flow through one language such as C++ is a useful start.
Data structures, algorithms, math, and debugging remain useful foundations as problems grow.
But the important point here is not how many syntax rules you know.
A strong programmer understands the game's intent and produces behavior the team can trust.

scenes.title: 2D Artist — Showing the Look of the Game
lines: 2D artists show the mood and shapes of a game's world visually.
Concept artists explore characters and environments and create visual guides for the team.
Depending on the project, artists may handle character illustrations, backgrounds, icons, interfaces, or sprite animation.
The work is not only about making a pretty picture; gameplay information must also read clearly.
They check whether enemies and allies are distinct and whether important objects disappear into the background.
Useful fundamentals include observation, simple forms, proportion, silhouette, composition, value, and color.
Artists create several quick directions and revise them repeatedly through feedback.
They must consider how an image will look and function inside the actual game screen, not only as a finished illustration.
2D art designs both a game's first impression and the information the player needs.

scenes.title: 3D Artist — Building a Playable World
lines: 3D artists create characters, environments, and props that can be viewed from every angle.
Modelers create form, while texture and material work defines surface color and feel.
Rigging and animation prepare characters and objects to move naturally.
Environment artists arrange assets and lighting to complete a space.
Games require artists to consider both visual quality and whether an asset moves and renders well.
They repeatedly check scale, orientation, movement, and readability inside the engine.
Useful fundamentals include form, proportion, spatial thinking, light, and materials.
It is usually better to finish a small prop such as a box or chair before attempting a complex character.
3D art does not stop at turning a drawing into a model; it connects the asset to a playable space.

scenes.title: Each Discipline Contains Many Roles
lines: We used four broad categories, but real teams have many more specialized jobs.
Design can include gameplay, systems, levels, interfaces, and user experience.
Programming can include gameplay, engines, graphics, networking, tools, and artificial intelligence.
Art can include concept, character, environment, animation, visual effects, and technical art.
The same job title may involve different work depending on the company and genre.
You do not need to memorize every specialization at the beginning.
Make something small and notice which kinds of problems are the most interesting to you.
Trying the whole pipeline once and then choosing one area to study deeply is a practical starting point.

scenes.title: Games Emerge Through Iteration Between Roles
lines: Production is not a sequence where design, programming, and art each finish once and close.
A designer defines a rule, then a programmer creates a form that can be tested quickly.
When art assets arrive, the team checks visuals and motion and finds problems through playtesting.
The results lead to more changes in rules, code, placement, and art.
Reducing wasted iteration requires the ability to explain your work and understand other roles' constraints.
When something breaks, it is more useful to show what changed in which situation than to look for someone to blame.
Solo developers cannot skip this process either; they simply change hats and ask the same questions alone.
Game development combines skill in each discipline with collaboration that connects every result into one playable experience.

scenes.title: The Smallest Step Toward Your Role
lines: If you do not know which role fits you, touch one tiny scene in four different ways.
If design interests you, summarize a familiar game's rules on one page and change one of them.
If programming interests you, make a character move and interact with one object.
If 2D art interests you, create a small character or icon set and check it at actual screen size.
If 3D art interests you, model a small prop and place it inside an engine.
A huge first project matters less than finishing a small result and explaining your contribution.
Record which problems felt exciting and which felt frustrating, and your preferred role will become clearer.
Loving games is a good starting point. Now discover how you want to use that interest to make them.
Which would you like to try first: design, programming, or art?
